question: CWIP growing 5 years while PP&E stays flat. Most likely indicates:
before: Normally CWIP transfers to PP&E on completion. CWIP rising without PP&E increase = projects stalled or costs parked to inflate profits. Classic red flag (Module 8). A would show PP&E rising too.
after:
Concept: CWIP (Capital Work-in-Progress) represents incomplete construction or asset development; upon completion, these costs transfer to PP&E (Property, Plant & Equipment). A mismatch between growing CWIP and flat PP&E over a multi-year period signals either stalled projects or accounting choices designed to defer expense recognition.

Why this is correct: When CWIP accumulates for 5 years without corresponding PP&E additions, it typically means either (1) projects have stalled and assets remain incomplete, blocking the transfer to the operational PP&E line, or (2) management is deliberately parking costs in CWIP (which appears as a non-current asset) rather than expensing them, artificially supporting operating profitability and asset base metrics. Both scenarios are red flags in equity research.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Aggressive capacity investment would show PP&E rising significantly as completed projects transfer from CWIP. Flat PP&E contradicts genuine expansion.

B) Assets being capitalised properly would result in CWIP transitioning smoothly to PP&E as projects finish. The 5-year divergence indicates improper deferral, not proper capitalisation.

D) Paying off debt has no direct relationship to CWIP or PP&E movements; this conflates balance-sheet structure (liabilities) with asset composition.

Intuition: In equity research, stalled CWIP is a classic indicator of project abandonment, cost overruns, or regulatory delays that management is masking from the P&L. It also reveals potential aggressive accounting—parking operating expenses into capital accounts to inflate near-term margins and return on assets. Always track the CWIP-to-PP&E conversion ratio year-over-year.
